language.name: English
cpu.title: CPU fully loaded
cpu.summary: The processor was almost fully busy for {0} s. Programs that need CPU time at that moment (games, audio, video calls) have to wait, which shows up as stutter or input lag.
cpu.ev.seconds: CPU load was at or above 90 % for {0} s in the analysed window
cpu.ev.baseline: Typical CPU load before the problem: {0} %
cpu.ev.top: Biggest CPU consumer: {0} (peak {1} % of all cores)
cpu.check.process: Check whether {0} is expected to run at this time (Task Manager > Details).
cpu.check.taskmanager: Open Task Manager and sort by CPU when it happens again.
cpu.check.background: If it recurs during games, close or limit background applications (browser tabs, launchers).
throttle.title: CPU clock speed dropped under load
throttle.summary: The processor ran well below its usual speed while it was busy. Typical causes are high temperatures, power limits, a power-saving plan or a laptop running on battery.
throttle.ev.baseline: Usual CPU speed before the problem: {0} % of nominal
throttle.ev.load: CPU load at the same time: {0} %
throttle.check.temp: Check CPU temperatures under load with a hardware monitor (e.g. HWiNFO).
throttle.check.power: Check the Windows power mode and, on laptops, whether the charger is connected.
disk.title: Storage overloaded
disk.summary: The drive was busy or responding slowly. Games that stream textures and programs that load files have to wait, which causes hitches and short freezes.
disk.ev.top: Most I/O by {0} (peak {1} MB/s, file and network I/O)
disk.check.resmon: Open Resource Monitor (resmon) > Disk to see which files are read or written.
disk.check.schedule: If a backup, sync or antivirus scan runs at that time, schedule it for when you are not using the PC.
mem.title: Memory running low
mem.summary: The PC was short on free memory and had to move data to and from the disk. That is much slower than RAM and causes freezes.
mem.ev.paging: Windows read {0} memory pages per second back from disk (paging)
mem.ev.top: Largest memory user: {0} ({1} MB private memory)
mem.check.close: Close memory-heavy programs (browsers with many tabs, editors, launchers) before gaming.
mem.check.ram: If this happens often, more RAM would help.
gpu.title: Graphics card at its limit
gpu.summary: The graphics card was fully loaded. In games this is often normal, but if the frame rate drops or stutters, the graphics settings may be too high for this card.
gpu.ev.seconds: GPU at or above 97 % for {0} s
gpu.check.settings: Lower resolution or demanding settings (ray tracing, shadows, textures) and compare.
gpu.check.limit: A frame-rate limit slightly below the monitor refresh rate often makes frame pacing smoother.
gpubg.title: Background program using the graphics card: {0}
gpubg.summary: While {0} was in front, other programs also used the GPU noticeably. They compete for GPU time and video memory.
gpubg.ev.process: {0} used {1} % of the GPU in the background
gpubg.check.close: Close or pause these programs (video playback, a local AI model, browser tabs with 3D content) and compare.
gpubg.check.acceleration: Turn off hardware acceleration in programs that do not need it.
known.tiworker: Windows Modules Installer Worker (installs Windows updates)
known.msiexec: Windows Installer (a program is being installed or updated)
known.wmi: WMI provider host (often triggered by monitoring tools)
known.steam: Steam client (possibly downloading or updating games)
known.epic: Epic Games Launcher (possibly downloading or updating)
known.ollama: Ollama (a local AI model is running)
known.ollama.runner: Ollama model runner (a local AI model is running)
bg.summary: A known background task was working when the problem happened. These tasks often start on a schedule and briefly take CPU, disk or network resources.
bg.check.schedule: Check whether the task runs on a schedule (Task Scheduler or the program's settings) and move it to a time you are not using the PC.
bg.check.security: Do not turn off security software; schedule its scans instead.
ping.ev.baseline: Usual ping to {0} before the problem: {1} ms
netlocal.title: Delay already between PC and router
netlocal.summary: Pings to your own router were slow or got lost. The problem is in your home network (Wi-Fi signal, interference, cable, router), not at your internet provider.
netlocal.summary.weak: Pings to your router were slow while the internet address answered normally. Some routers answer pings with low priority, so this is only a weak sign of a home-network problem.
netlocal.check.wifi: On Wi-Fi: move closer to the router, use 5 or 6 GHz, or try a network cable for comparison.
netlocal.check.router: Restart the router and check whether other devices use a lot of bandwidth at the same time.
netremote.title: Network delay beyond your router
netremote.summary: Your home network answered normally, but the connection to the internet was slow or lost packets. The cause is probably at your internet provider or further along the route, not on your PC.
netremote.summary.unknown: The connection to the internet was slow or lost packets. WhyLag could not ping your router, so it cannot tell whether the cause is local or at the provider.
netremote.ev.router: Router answered normally during the problem
netremote.ev.router.max: Router answered normally during the problem (max {0} ms)
netremote.check.provider: If it happens often, note the times and contact your internet provider with this report.
netremote.check.target: Check whether it also happens with another test address, e.g. your game server (Settings > Network).
bloat.title: Own {0} slowed down the connection (bufferbloat)
bloat.summary: Latency rose exactly while this PC was using a lot of {0} bandwidth. When a line is full, routers queue packets, so game and call traffic has to wait. This is called bufferbloat.
bloat.ev.traffic: Your PC's {0} at the same time: {1} Mbit/s
bloat.ev.top: Most I/O at that moment by {0} ({1} MB/s, file and network I/O)
bloat.check.pause: Pause large {0}s (cloud sync, game updates, streaming) while gaming.
bloat.check.sqm: If your router supports Smart Queue Management (SQM), turning it on usually fixes this.
retrans.title: Network data had to be resent ({0} %)
retrans.summary: A noticeable share of the data this PC sent had to be sent again because packets were lost or arrived too late. Typical causes are a weak Wi-Fi signal, a faulty cable or an overloaded line.
retrans.ev.peak: {0} % of sent TCP segments were resent ({1} per second)
retrans.check.cable: Try a network cable or a different Wi-Fi band; replace old cables.
retrans.check.drivers: Update the network adapter driver and router firmware.
stall.title: The whole system froze briefly
stall.summary: WhyLag records once per second. At this point it could not run on time, so Windows itself was not scheduling programs normally. Common causes are driver problems, storage hangs or extreme memory pressure.
stall.ev.gap: Recording paused for {0} ms longer than planned
stall.check.others: Look at the other findings and event log entries at the same time.
stall.check.drivers: Update chipset, storage and graphics drivers. The driver latency analysis in Settings can name a blocking driver.
dpc.core.title: Drivers kept a CPU core busy ({0} %)
dpc.core.summary: One CPU core spent a lot of time in driver routines (DPCs and interrupts). Nothing else can run on that core meanwhile, which causes audio crackles, input lag and hitches.
dpc.core.ev.dpc: DPC time on the busiest core: {0} %
dpc.core.ev.isr: Interrupt time on the busiest core: {0} %
dpc.check.helper: Turn on the driver latency analysis in Settings to see which driver it is.
dpc.check.drivers: Update network, Wi-Fi, audio, storage and graphics drivers.
dpc.title: Driver {0} blocked the CPU for {1} ms
dpc.summary: A driver ({0}) ran for an unusually long time in one go. During that time the CPU core could not run anything else, which causes audio crackles, input lag and hitches.
dpc.ev.driver: {0} ({1}) ran for {2} µs in one go
dpc.check.update: Update the driver behind {0} (device manufacturer's website or Windows Update).
dpc.check.power: Disabling unused devices (e.g. Bluetooth, extra network adapters) and power-saving for the device can help.
driver.wdf: driver framework (often USB or Bluetooth devices)
events.generic.title: Errors in the Windows event log at the same time
events.generic.summary: Windows logged errors close to the problem. They are not necessarily the cause, but worth a look.
events.generic.check: Open Event Viewer (eventvwr) and look at the listed entries around this time.
events.tdr.title: Graphics driver stopped responding and recovered
events.tdr.summary: Windows reset the graphics driver because it stopped responding. The screen freezes or goes black for a moment when this happens.
events.tdr.check: Update or cleanly reinstall the graphics driver. Remove GPU overclocks or undervolts for testing.
events.whea.title: Hardware error reported (WHEA)
events.whea.summary: Windows recorded a hardware error. Even corrected errors can cause stutters; repeated ones point to unstable overclocking, power or failing hardware.
events.whea.check: Reset CPU/RAM overclocks and EXPO/XMP for testing and check the event details in Event Viewer.
events.storage.title: Storage error or timeout
events.storage.summary: A drive did not answer in time or reported an error. Programs that read from it freeze until it responds.
events.storage.check: Check the drive's health (e.g. CrystalDiskInfo) and cables, and update storage drivers and SSD firmware.
events.lowmem.title: Windows ran low on virtual memory
events.lowmem.summary: Windows warned that memory was nearly exhausted and named the largest consumers in the event.
events.lowmem.check: Close the programs named in the event and check the page file settings.
events.hang.title: A program stopped responding
events.hang.summary: Windows recorded that a program hung at this time.
events.hang.check: Check whether the program named in the event has an update.
events.crash.title: A program crashed
events.crash.summary: Windows recorded a program crash at this time.
events.crash.check: Check whether the program named in the event has an update.
events.wlan.title: Wi-Fi connection changed
events.wlan.summary: Windows recorded a Wi-Fi disconnect, reconnect or roaming event. While this happens, network traffic stalls.
events.wlan.check: Use a stable band (5 or 6 GHz), check the signal strength or try a network cable.
events.update.title: Windows Update was working
events.update.summary: Windows Update downloaded or installed something at this time, which uses disk, CPU and network.
events.update.check: Set active hours in Windows Update so installations happen when you are not using the PC.
frames.title: {0} stuttered: a frame took {1} ms
frames.summary: The game really hitched: single frames took several times longer than usual. This confirms what you noticed; the other findings show what the PC was busy with at that moment.
frames.ev.seconds: Seconds with hitches in the analysed window: {0}
frames.check.game: If no other finding explains it, the hitch may come from the game itself (shader compilation, loading). Check whether it happens at the same spot again.
frames.check.limit: A frame-rate limit slightly below your monitor's refresh rate often makes frame pacing smoother.
fpsdrop.title: {0}: frame rate dropped to {1} fps
fpsdrop.summary: The frame rate fell to half or less of its usual value for several seconds.
fpsdrop.check: Compare with the other findings: a full GPU points to graphics settings, a full CPU or disk to background load.
wifi.summary: The Wi-Fi connection was weaker or less stable than usual. Even when pings look fine, this can cause short lag spikes.
wifi.summary.router: The Wi-Fi connection was unstable and the router responded slowly at the same time. This is a typical cause of lag spikes in online games and calls.
wifi.ev.roam: Wi-Fi switched to another access point (roaming)
wifi.ev.rate: Wi-Fi link speed fell to {0} Mbit/s (usually {1} Mbit/s)
wifi.check.position: Move the PC or router, avoid walls and metal in between, or use a network cable for comparison.
wifi.check.node: If the PC switches between access points or mesh nodes, connect it to one fixed band or node.
ai.cloud: '{0}' is an Ollama cloud model. WhyLag only uses models that run on this PC.
ai.nomodel: No local model is installed in Ollama. Choose one in Settings > Local AI.
ai.nothing: There are no findings, so there is nothing the AI could explain without guessing.
ai.rejected: The AI answer could not be verified against the recorded evidence, so it is not shown. The rule-based findings are unaffected.
ai.timeout: Ollama did not answer in time.

Details were written to {1}.
app.incident.none: Nothing unusual found in the recorded data.
app.running: WhyLag is already running. You find it in the notification area of the taskbar.
app.started.text: Press {0} when something stutters or lags.
app.started.title: WhyLag is recording
chart.nodata: No recorded data for this incident.
err.eventlog: No event log channel could be opened.
err.helper.declined: The driver latency helper was not started because administrator approval was declined.
err.helper.stopped: The driver latency helper stopped. Another tool may be using the Windows kernel trace (e.g. LatencyMon).
err.kernel.admin: Driver latency measurement needs administrator rights.
err.kernel.busy: The Windows kernel trace is already used by another tool (e.g. a profiler or LatencyMon). Close it and try again.
err.presentmon.hash: The downloaded PresentMon file does not match the expected checksum and was deleted.
err.presentmon.stopped: PresentMon stopped repeatedly. Frame times are not recorded.
model.note.8b: Best explanations; needs about 8 GB VRAM for fast answers.
model.note.4b: Good balance for most PCs, also usable on the CPU.
model.note.license: Alternative small model; check the license terms.
model.note.small: For weak PCs; shorter, simpler explanations.
report.ai.note: Generated by a local language model from the findings above. Only statements backed by recorded evidence are shown.
report.ai.title: Explanation by local AI ({0})
report.disclaimer: WhyLag shows what happened at the same time – a strong hint, not proof of the cause.
report.none.text: None of WhyLag's checks found anything unusual in the analysed seconds. The cause may be outside what WhyLag measures, e.g. inside the game, on the game server, or shorter than a second.
report.none.title: Nothing unusual found

set.ai.nomodels: Download a model below to use AI explanations.
set.ai.norecommend: This PC has little memory, so AI explanations are not recommended. Everything else works normally.
set.ai.notlocal: Note: this address is not this PC.
set.ai.recommend: Suggested for this PC: {0} – about {1} GB download, license {2}. {3}
set.ai.text: WhyLag works fully without AI. If enabled, a model running on this PC via Ollama explains the findings in plain language – only when you click 'Explain', only with the findings and measured values, and every statement is checked against the evidence. Cloud models are never used.
set.autodetect: Detect freezes, hitches and network spikes automatically
set.autostart: Start WhyLag when I sign in to Windows
set.data.deleteall.confirm: Delete all {0} saved incidents? This cannot be undone.
set.data.deleted: All incidents were deleted. Reopen the WhyLag window to refresh the list.
set.data.reset.confirm: Reset all settings to their defaults? Saved incidents are kept.
set.err.address: The Ollama address is not valid. The default is http://127.0.0.1:11434
set.err.buffer: History must be between 1 and 120 minutes.
set.err.hotkey: Please enter a hotkey with at least one modifier, e.g. Ctrl+Alt+L.
set.frames.notpermitted: Permission missing: allow frame-time capture once (administrator approval, then sign out and in).
set.frames.permission.confirm:
Frame-time capture uses Windows event tracing, which is reserved for administrators and the built-in group "Performance Log Users".

WhyLag can add your account to that group. Windows asks for administrator approval; the change takes effect after signing out and in.

Command:
{0}

You can undo it in Computer Management > Local Users and Groups.
set.frames.permission.done: Done. Sign out of Windows and in again, then frame times are recorded.
set.frames.permission.failed: The change did not succeed. You can run the command in an administrator PowerShell.
set.frames.text: With Intel PresentMon (free, MIT license) WhyLag sees every frame of the game in front and can confirm stutters and frame-rate drops. It only runs while WhyLag runs.
set.general.text: History is kept in memory. Something is written to disk only when an incident is captured.
set.latency.confirm:
To name drivers that block the CPU, WhyLag starts a small helper with administrator rights each time WhyLag starts. Windows asks for approval.

The helper only reads the Windows kernel trace for driver timings, sends nothing but these measurements to WhyLag and ends together with it.
set.latency.enable: Name drivers that block the CPU (asks for administrator approval when WhyLag starts)
set.latency.text: Without administrator rights WhyLag sees how busy each CPU core is with drivers (DPC/interrupt time). With the optional helper it also measures how long each driver runs and names it – the typical cause of audio crackles and input lag.
set.network.target.tip: An IP address or host name, e.g. 1.1.1.1 or your game server
set.network.text: WhyLag pings your router and one internet address once per second to tell home-network problems from provider problems – its only internet connection. Wi-Fi values and TCP retransmissions are read locally; network names are never stored.
set.title: Settings

ui.ai.intro.off: A language model on this PC (via Ollama) can explain the findings above in plain language. It only receives the findings and their measured values, and every statement is checked against the evidence. WhyLag works fully without it.

ui.howto: Keep WhyLag running in the background. When a game stutters, a call freezes or the PC hangs, press {0}: WhyLag saves the last minutes and shows what happened at that moment.
ui.howto.auto: Freezes, hitches and network spikes are also detected automatically.
ui.howto.autooff: Automatic detection is off in Settings.
ui.howto.title: How to use WhyLag
ui.live.subtitle: What WhyLag is recording right now. The last minute is shown; the full history stays in memory.
ui.noincidents: No incidents yet. Press the hotkey the next time something lags, or add a demo.
ui.patterns.none: No recurring pattern yet. Patterns appear when the same cause shows up in at least 3 incidents at different times.

ui.timeline.legend: Shaded: analysed window · dashed: reported · dots: lost pings
warn.counters: Some Windows performance counters are missing or damaged, so a few metrics are not recorded. "lodctr /R" in an administrator command prompt usually repairs them.
warn.presentmon.missing: PresentMon is not installed, so frame times are not recorded. You can download it in Settings.
warn.presentmon.permission: Frame-time capture needs administrator rights or the 'Performance Log Users' group. Settings can set this up.
warn.process: Per-process counters are unavailable, so WhyLag cannot name the programs causing load.
warn.wifi.location: Wi-Fi details are not available. If you use Wi-Fi, allow desktop apps to access your location in Windows privacy settings.

ui.table.deleteconfirm: Delete {0} incident(s)? This cannot be undone.

ui.events.none: No warnings or errors were logged by Windows during the recorded minutes.
ui.note.title: Your note
ui.note.hint: What were you doing, and what turned out to be the cause? Saved with the incident and included in exported reports.
ui.ignoreapp.confirm: Hitches in {0} will no longer start automatic incidents. You can undo this in Settings → Frame times.
set.ignored.tip: Process names, separated by commas, e.g. brave, webwallpaper64. Browsers and wallpaper apps are ignored automatically.
app.incident.summary: {0} new lag reports recorded. Click to open WhyLag.
growth.title: {0} grew by {1} GB over the last hours
growth.summary: Memory use of this process keeps rising without falling back. That looks like a memory leak: Windows has to page out memory, which causes stutter.
growth.ev.start: {0} used {1} MB at the start of the recording
growth.ev.free: Only {0} % of memory is still free
growth.check.restart: Restart {0} – if the stutter disappears, the leak is confirmed.
growth.check.update: Check for an update of the program; memory leaks are often fixed quickly.
household.title: Another device in your network was using the {0}
household.summary: The router counted much more traffic than this PC caused. Someone else (streaming, downloads, backups, updates) filled the line at the moment of the lag.
household.ev.router: Router total: {0} Mbit/s down, {1} Mbit/s up
household.ev.pc: This PC: {0} Mbit/s down, {1} Mbit/s up
household.check.devices: Check which devices were active at that time (router web interface, list of connected devices).
overlay.tip: Drag to move · right-click to close
session.notify.title: Session report: {0}
session.nocauses: No lag reports in this session.
session.none: No sessions yet. A session is saved automatically when you play a fullscreen game for at least 5 minutes.

set.temperatures: Read temperatures from HWiNFO or LibreHardwareMonitor if one of them is running
set.router: Read total traffic from the router via UPnP (shows if other devices fill the line)
warn.router: No router with UPnP traffic counters found. Enable UPnP on the router or turn off router traffic in the settings.
temp.summary: At this temperature the chip lowers its clock speed to protect itself (thermal throttling), which costs performance.
temp.check.cooling: Clean dust from heatsinks and fans; check that the cooler sits firmly.
temp.check.fans: Check the fan curve and case airflow; laptops benefit from a hard, flat surface.
ui.sessions.subtitle: A short report for every gaming session of at least 5 minutes.
ui.changes.subtitle: Driver and Windows updates after which lag happened clearly more often.
ui.changes.none: No update made lag noticeably worse.
ui.changes.detail: {0} lag reports in {1} days afterwards, {2} in {3} days before
